query: Design a hypothesis to achieve coercive field ($H_c$) values exceeding 100 Oe in an fcc-based high-entropy alloy containing Ti. The operating regime of interest involves magnetic ordering temperatures significantly above room temperature. The known failure mode in existing single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni systems is a suppression of the orbital moment leading to low coercivity. Propose a design constraint involving the introduction of a secondary phase or specific chemical interaction that could alter the magnetic ground state or coupling without disrupting the fcc matrix, and describe a falsification experiment to distinguish between single-phase and dual-phase magnetic contributions.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanoscale, coherent L12-ordered Fe-Ti precipitate phase within an fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn high-entropy alloy matrix will enhance the coercive field ($H_c$) to exceed 100 Oe by pinning domain walls via magneto-elastic strain fields and creating a hard-magnetic/soft-magnetic exchange-spring interface, while maintaining the high Curie temperature of the fcc matrix.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn high-entropy alloy with suppressed orbital moment, low anisotropy, and coercivity significantly below 100 Oe, exhibiting ferromagnetic ordering well above room temperature.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging of the alloy at temperatures between 600°C and 800°C for durations sufficient to nucleate and grow coherent L12-ordered Fe-Ti intermetallic precipitates (approx. 5-20 nm) without inducing bulk phase separation or loss of the fcc matrix continuity.
generation.conditions: Aging atmosphere: High vacuum or inert argon to prevent oxidation; Post-aging cooling rate: Controlled furnace cooling to room temperature to preserve precipitate coherency.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent lattice mismatch strain fields at the fcc matrix/L12-precipitate interface and the formation of a hard-magnetic L12-FeTi phase with higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy than the soft fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as strong pinning centers for magnetic domain walls due to local variations in magnetocrystalline anisotropy and magneto-elastic coupling. The interaction between the soft fcc matrix and the harder L12-FeTi precipitates creates an exchange-spring mechanism where the pinning energy required to depin the domain wall exceeds the thermal energy at room temperature, thereby increasing $H_c$ without significantly reducing the saturation magnetization or Curie temperature of the bulk material.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy will exhibit a coercive field $H_c > 100$ Oe, a squareness ratio ($M_r/M_s$) greater than 0.3, and a Curie temperature ($T_c$) remaining above 400 K, with the magnetic hysteresis loop showing a distinct 'kink' indicative of exchange coupling between phases.
generation.baseline: The unaged, single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Ti alloy which exhibits $H_c < 20$ Oe due to low anisotropy and the absence of pinning sites.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds only if the precipitates remain coherent or semi-coherent; if the precipitates grow beyond 50 nm or become incoherent, the pinning efficiency drops, and $H_c$ may decrease. The Ti concentration must be sufficient to form the precipitate but not so high as to destabilize the fcc matrix into a brittle BCC phase.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact crystal structure and magnetic moment of the Fe-Ti phase at the nanoscale within this specific high-entropy environment; it is possible that the Ti atoms might segregate to grain boundaries rather than forming a distinct precipitate phase, or that the high entropy of the matrix suppresses the formation of the ordered L12-FeTi phase entirely.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the Fe-Co-Ni-Mn-Ti alloy: Batch A (aged to induce precipitates) and Batch B (quenched rapidly to retain single-phase fcc). Perform high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm the presence and size of L12-ordered Fe-Ti precipitates in Batch A. Then, measure the magnetic hysteresis loops of both batches at 300 K and 77 K. Additionally, perform a magnetic force microscopy (MFM) study on Batch A to map domain wall pinning sites.
measurements: Precipitate size distribution and volume fraction via APT/HRTEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if Batch A exhibits $H_c < 100$ Oe despite the confirmed presence of coherent L12-ordered Fe-Ti precipitates (5-20 nm), or if Batch B (single-phase) exhibits $H_c > 100$ Oe due to some other mechanism, or if the precipitates in Batch A are found to be incoherent, amorphous, or of a different crystal structure (e.g., B2) that does not support the proposed strain-field mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .
